content: The World Health Organization (WHO) will utilize specific communication channels to disseminate information about the global situation. These communications will be integrated into the International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005) framework and shared with National IHR Focal Points, Disease Outbreak News releases, and various public and media platforms, including social media. During the interpandemic phase, which is the period between influenza pandemics, heightened vigilance and thorough risk assessments at local, national, and global levels are essential. If risk assessments indicate that a new virus is unlikely to develop into a pandemic strain, activities may be scaled back to those typical of the interpandemic phase. The pandemic phase refers to the global spread of human influenza caused by a new subtype. Transitions between the interpandemic, alert, and pandemic phases can occur rapidly or gradually, depending on global risk assessments based on virological, epidemiological, and clinical data. In the transition phase, as global risk decreases, global actions may be scaled down, and countries may shift their focus toward recovery activities based on their own risk assessments. The global phases and their application in risk management are distinct from the declaration of a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) under the IHR (2005) or the declaration of a pandemic. These determinations are based on specific assessments and are used to communicate the need for collective global action or to fulfill regulatory, legal, or contractual obligations. The responsibility for determining a PHEIC lies with the WHO Director-General under Article 12 of the IHR (2005). Similarly, the declaration of a pandemic may be made by the WHO Director-General during the global spread of human influenza caused by a new subtype, as appropriate to the situation. While these declarations may trigger regulatory actions by WHO and Member States, national-level actions should be based on local risk assessments and proportionate to the risk. The continuum of pandemic phases—encompassing preparedness, response, and recovery—follows a global average of cases over time, informed by ongoing risk assessments and aligned with broader emergency risk management frameworks. The IHR (2005) Annex 2 includes human influenza caused by a new subtype as one of the diseases that must be reported to WHO under all circumstances due to its potential public health impact. WHO's actions throughout the pandemic phases are guided by global risk assessments, while national actions are informed by local risk assessments. The decoupling of national actions from global phases is necessary, as the global risk assessment does not necessarily reflect the situation in individual Member States. The framework involves Member States, industry, and other stakeholders in a global approach to pandemic preparedness and response. It includes three core components: virus sharing, benefit sharing, and governance. Standard Material Transfer Agreements (SMTAs) outline the rights and obligations of laboratories within the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) when transferring PIP biological materials. This includes binding contracts with non-GISRS recipients, annual contributions from influenza vaccine manufacturers, and other benefits such as laboratory capacity building and the establishment of antiviral and vaccine stockpiles. The governance of the PIP Framework includes oversight by the World Health Assembly, implementation promotion by the WHO Director-General, and guidance from an Advisory Group. WHO acts as the secretariat, working with public and private partners to achieve results efficiently. GISRS plays a critical role in monitoring circulating influenza viruses, detecting new strains with pandemic potential, and supporting vaccine development. Member States are responsible for timely sharing of influenza viruses with pandemic potential, contributing to the benefit-sharing system, and supporting GISRS. WHO provides biannual recommendations on seasonal influenza vaccine composition and reviews vaccine candidates for pandemic potential. Emergency risk management for health (ERMH) focuses on managing risks from acute hazards, including pandemics, chemical spills, and natural disasters. It aims to strengthen country and community capacities, integrate risk management into health systems, and advocate for health aspects in national and international policies. ERMH is guided by principles such as comprehensive risk management, an all-hazards approach, multisectoral collaboration, community resilience, sustainable development, and ethical considerations. Effective pandemic preparedness requires a whole-of-society approach, involving coordinated efforts across public and private sectors. Business continuity planning is essential to mitigate potential disruptions caused by pandemics. WHO supports Member States in strengthening core capacities, developing national vaccine policies, and increasing global production capacity for pandemic vaccines. Planning and coordination are critical for effective emergency risk management. WHO advocates for collaboration among UN organizations, development agencies, and other stakeholders to enhance early detection, reporting, and research on influenza outbreaks with pandemic potential.
